rv.q: It is quick and inspired thinking from the National: this play deserves a far longer life on stage and on screen.
The play remains admirably, unapologetically angry, a timely articulation of an ongoing struggle for love, dignity and acceptance.
This night snatched at the National in the very maw of lockdown reminds us what we’ve been missing.

It’s a compelling, charismatic performance in a witty, powerful play that, though slightly overpacked with issues, raises searching questions about acceptance, belonging and deep-rooted racism — and about the way national identity interplays with historical legacy.
It's a blazing powerhouse of a turn and suggests an NT raring to get going again.
The play begins fuelled by fury, but it ends in unexpected hope.
The piece isn’t quite as successful, to be honest.
This is vital, urgent theatre, unflinchingly confronting our present, and setting its sights on the future.
It's a charismatic performance at the heart of an urgent play.
Balogun is by turns defiant, confiding, fierce and defenseless, all with a tightly focused, high-energy performance that zips along, driving Delroy's many-voiced narrative at the speed of thought.

For now, one can only applaud the "welcome blast of positivity" in artistic director Rufus Norris's words that this reopening however briefly was able to represent and to predict that Delroy remains far too vital a figure to be absent from us for long.
